query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Oxide-scale formation driven by partial pressure of oxygen (or reducing gas activity) leads to selective Al–Ti–Cr depletion at near-surface layers of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3, causing embrittling secondary phases and microcracks that culminate in sudden failure at high temperature.
generation.material_initial_state: As-printed Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an FCC matrix, as produced by additive manufacturing methods (e.g., laser powder bed fusion).
generation.intervention: Systematically vary oxygen or hydrogen partial pressure during isothermal exposures at 600–800 °C and track weight changes, oxide-scale composition, and crack formation under mechanical loading.
generation.conditions: (1) 600–800 °C exposure in controlled atmospheres from near-vacuum (very low O2) to ambient air, with separate trials under reducing (H2) conditions as a comparison. (2) Comparable inert-environment exposures as the baseline.
generation.structural_mediator: Progressive formation of multi-element spinel/halite-type oxides and sub-surface depletion of Al, Ti, and Cr, yielding brittle intermetallic or sigma-like phases near grain boundaries, promoting microcracking.
generation.mechanism: Under sufficiently high pO2 or high H2 activity, local oxidation/reduction triggers reactive element migration to the alloy–environment interface, forming thick or spalling oxide scales and depletion zones that lead to crack initiation and premature failure under mechanical stress.
generation.predicted_outcome: When the alloy is exposed to higher oxygen partial pressures at 600–800 °C, one observes (i) accelerated weight gain from thicker oxide scales, (ii) a higher frequency of near-surface elemental depletion and secondary phase formation, and (iii) an increased propensity for cracks and catastrophic fracture compared to lower pO2 or inert/reducing conditions.
generation.baseline: Minimal oxide film and limited microcracking in inert-atmosphere exposures at the same temperatures (600–800 °C).
generation.boundary: Durations of ≤100 h, temperatures 600–800 °C, and pO2 spanning from nominal vacuum to ambient pressure. Longer exposure times or higher temperatures would exacerbate oxide growth and embrittlement.
generation.uncertainty: Whether reduced Al–Ti content can form a stable protective layer under certain partial pressures or if doping levels suffice for an intact alumina-based scale is unclear without further kinetic data.

falsification_experiment.design: Expose identically processed specimens to controlled 600–800 °C environments at systematically varied O2/H2 partial pressures. Perform parallel inert (low pO2) exposures as controls. Monitor mass gain via TGA, microstructure via SEM–EDS–XRD, and mechanical response by either small-scale bend or tensile tests post-exposure.
measurements: Oxide chemistry and morphology by SEM–EDS, XRD.
Elemental depth profiles across oxide–metal interface.
Fracture mode and critical failure loads or strains after exposure.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no substantial difference arises in oxide scale thickness, element depletion, or mechanical failure modes under different O2/H2 partial pressures—and no correlation is found between catastrophic cracking and near-surface compositional changes—then the proposed depletion-driven embrittlement mechanism must be rejected or revised.

The formation of corundom (Mn2O3) during the experiment can be explained with the increase in temperature, and the initially formed corundom oxide changed to spinel (Mn3O4) at a higher temperature (950 °C). If considering oxides that form at a higher temperature such as 950, 1000, and 1050 °C, the ThermoCalc-predicted spinel oxide type is the same as the experimentally found spinel oxide. chosen.conditions: 600–800 °C with varying O2/H2 to track oxidation kinetics and microstructural evolution relative to baseline
chosen.why: Systematically varying gas composition and temperature in a controlled-exposure experiment directly tests the hypothesized mechanism of oxidation or reduction-driven microstructural degradation. Monitoring mass changes and analyzing oxide-scale formation and element depletion/segregation under different environmental conditions can verify whether local reactions lead to embrittlement and catastrophic failure. These standard materials-science techniques provide the clearest path to falsifying or confirming the proposed mechanism.
